planting.note: Plant one Lord male shrub for every six to eight fruiting females, such as Sunny or Leikora, within about 50 feet for reliable pollen transfer in full sun on well-drained soil.

directions: Lord is a hardy male sea buckthorn selection grown solely to supply pollen, since Hippophae rhamnoides is dioecious and fruits only when a male plant blooms nearby. It opens its small, petal-less catkins early and holds bloom for roughly ten days, long enough to overlap with most early- and mid-season female cultivars. Give it the same lean, sandy, well-drained site the females need, since it shares their nitrogen-fixing roots and dislikes rich, wet soil. Position it upwind of the planting block where practical to help wind-borne pollen reach the widest number of female shrubs.
sources: Hardy Fruit Tree Nursery — Sea Buckthorn Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring within about 50 feet of another late-blooming Yezberry selection, such as Keiko, since Maxie will not set fruit on its own.

directions: Maxie is a Japanese-type haskap bred by Oregon State University's Dr. Maxine Thompson and released under the Yezberry name for its unusually large, olive-shaped fruit, among the biggest of any honeyberry selection. It blooms later than Russian-derived haskaps, which lets it dodge most late-spring frosts and lines its flowering up with the other Yezberry cultivars it needs for cross-pollination. Give it well-drained, slightly acidic soil and afternoon shade in hot summer areas, since intense heat can scald the ripening fruit. Established plants tolerate winter cold to roughly -40F but need consistent moisture through fruit set to size up properly.
sources: Proven Winners ColorChoice — Yezberry Cultural Data

planting.note: Plant within about 30 feet of another late-blooming haskap, such as Yezberry Maxie, in full sun on well-drained soil; Keiko flowers late enough to rely on active bee populations for pollination.

directions: Keiko belongs to the Japanese emphyllocalyx type of haskap and is among the latest-ripening honeyberries available, holding its rounded, heart-shaped fruit into late June or early July when most other cultivars have already finished. The delayed bloom is an asset in areas with unpredictable late frosts, since flowers open once pollinating insects are already active, which tends to improve fruit set. Plant in slightly acidic, well-drained soil and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer, and expect a spreading, twiggy bush that needs little pruning beyond removing dead wood in the first several years.
sources: One Green World Nursery — Keiko Honeyberry Notes

planting.note: Plant alongside an early-blooming pollinizer of similar bloom time, such as Blue Banana, since Happy Giant is self-infertile; space plants 3-4 feet apart in full sun on well-drained soil.

directions: Happy Giant is a Russian-derived F3 selection valued for producing some of the largest fruit of any haskap, elongated berries reaching over an inch long with a sweet-tart, blueberry-like flavor and high sugar content at harvest. It blooms early and tolerates winter cold to roughly -40F, but the early flowers benefit from a sheltered site or row cover during hard late frosts. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and expect a vigorous, upright bush that reaches significant yields by its fourth or fifth growing season. Fruit ripens ahead of strawberries, giving gardeners one of the earliest fresh harvests of the season.
sources: AgriForest Bio-Technologies — Happy Giant Haskap Notes

planting.note: Plant in full sun to light shade in moisture-retentive, fertile soil; Samdal is partially self-fertile but crops more heavily with a second Sambucus nigra cultivar nearby for wind pollination.

directions: Samdal is a Danish commercial black elderberry selection bred for unusually large flower and fruit clusters, giving a heavier harvest per bush than most older European elder cultivars. New shoots emerge vigorously from the crown each season and typically fruit the following year, so renewal pruning should favor one- and two-year canes while removing the oldest, least productive wood each dormant season. The lush green foliage and broad, creamy-white flower umbels make it attractive as a dual-purpose fruiting hedge as well as a productive orchard shrub. Berries ripen dark and glossy in late summer and are used for syrup, wine, and jelly, but like all elderberry, fruit should be cooked before eating and never consumed with the stems, leaves, or unripe berries attached.

planting.note: Plant in full to half-day sun in fertile, well-drained soil; foliage color develops darkest with strong sun exposure, and a second Sambucus nigra cultivar nearby improves fruit set.

directions: Thundercloud is grown chiefly as an ornamental elder, its deeply cut, dramatic burgundy-purple foliage set off by broad flat-topped clusters of bright pink flowers in early summer that mature into small dark purple-black berries by late summer. The rich leaf color holds best with several hours of direct sun daily and can fade toward green in heavy shade. Cut a portion of the oldest stems to the ground each winter to keep the naturally arching habit compact and to encourage the strongest, most vividly colored new growth, since the best foliage color appears on vigorous young canes. Berries are edible once fully ripe and cooked but are secondary to the shrub's landscape value here.
